description:
BoboMimi — One Earth. Every Sense. Everyone.

Team BoboMimi is two colleagues from Bintulu, Malaysia, taking on The Earth Information Jukebox challenge. Our project, TerraJuke, turns NASA Earth visualizations into multisensory experiences that can be heard, seen, read and felt, so that Earth science is accessible to everyone.

We welcome collaborators with experience in accessibility, sound design, data visualization and science communication.
summary: TerraJuke is a web jukebox that turns NASA's Earth Information Center visualizations into music you can play, touch and understand. Each "record" is a NASA Scientific Visualization Studio picture: climate warming, night lights, the air we share, ocean heat, Arctic sea ice, a century of temperature change and lightning seen from the Space Station. Press Play and the browser reads the picture's own colours, often back to real values on NASA's printed colour bars, and turns them into sound live, on fixed scales: warmer water plays higher, less sea ice plays lower. Side B of each record lets you touch a place to hear its story. Every note is also written as text, controls work with a keyboard and screen reader, and a 5W1H card says what you hear, who made the data, when, where, why and how. TerraJuke brings NASA's Earth pictures to people who cannot see them, and makes every visitor listen more closely to a changing planet.
details:
What it does. TerraJuke is a jukebox of NASA's Earth. Home introduces the project; Listen is the jukebox: eight records on a 3D shelf, a player, Play the whole jukebox (every record in turn), Mystery Record (guess a record by ear), and Your Record (turn a personal image into sound; it never leaves the device). Source code: https://github.com/Yoriichi-0u0/TerraJuke-The-Earth-Information-Jukebox

How it works. Everything runs in the browser with the Web Audio API; there are no recordings.

Climate Spiral (SVS 5190): Side A scans the picture's brightness and colour; Side B plays NASA GISTEMP v4 measurements on a fixed scale.

Night Lights (SVS 5313, EIC Version): colours read on NASA's legend (more light rises, less light falls); Side B plays NASA's twelve yearly frames, cross-checked against SVS 5276.

The Air We Share (SVS 5669): four aerosols, read from NASA's colour bar, play four instruments on a mixing desk.

Currents of Heat (SVS 3912): each current's colour is read back to °C on NASA's 0–32 °C bar, pole to pole.

Moving Earth: an Earth Information Center exhibit animation, sampled frame by frame.

The Ice Year (SVS 5046): NASA's own render camera, stored in each frame, lets us measure the sea ice NASA drew each month of 2024 in km²; Side B plays any Arctic place's ice season.

The Warming Map (SVS 5450): every map colour read back to a temperature anomaly on NASA's −2 to +2 °C bar; the global means read from colour match NASA's GISTEMP within 0.06 °C on average.

Storm Drums (SVS 5011): lightning detected by the ISS Lightning Imaging Sensor, counted from NASA's dots in every place; each month opens with a note for the world's lightning, then drums sweep west to east. Tests confirm about three quarters of it falls over land and that the storm belt follows the sun north and back.

Balancing data and music. Pitches come only from the data, on fixed pentatonic scales so layers stay musical. Tempo, timbre and the Sound setting (note by note, or one continuous gliding line) are labelled musical choices that never change which value made which note.

Accessibility. Captions and polite screen-reader announcements for every note; every map is a keyboard instrument; reduced motion stops all animation and 3D has 2D fallbacks; light and dark themes pass automated WCAG 2.1 AA checks. We have not run a user study and claim no learning gains or certification.

Validity. Every NASA file is pinned with its source URL, retrieval date and SHA-256; every mapping has unit tests that check readings against known facts (the Arctic warms fastest, the North Pole keeps its ice, the warm pool is warmest). 147 unit tests and 177 browser tests run before every release.

Tools. TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Three.js with react-three-fiber, Anime.js, lucide-react, Web Audio API, Playwright and axe-core for testing, Vercel for hosting, macOS sips, cwebp and ffmpeg for preparing NASA images.

Use of AI (SI). The team chose the concept, the NASA sources and every product decision. Code, tests and documentation were written with AI coding assistants under our direction: Anthropic Claude (Claude Code) for most of the application, and OpenAI Codex/ChatGPT earlier in development. The TerraJuke icon, artwork and vinyl surface were generated with ChatGPT image generation and carry a visible "AI-GENERATED" watermark or "AI" badge. In the app, no sound is AI-generated: all audio is synthesized live from NASA's data by our code. In the demo video the music is that live app sound and the narration voice is AI text-to-speech (Kokoro), as stated in the video's description and file metadata. No data is AI-generated, and no NASA logos or insignia are used.
